title: This Is What The Oldest Whale in The World Can Do
fullText: In 2007, a group of Anupia hunters in northern Alaska legally hunted a bowhead whale off the coast. But as they were cutting deep into the blubber of the whale's neck, their tools hit something hard. They had struck solid metal. It was completely fused with the tissue around it and clearly very old. They sent it over to historians to figure out exactly what it was, and the results didn't make any sense. The object was a bomblance tip and it was manufactured in New Bedford, Massachusetts in 1880, which means this exact harpoon was fired into this exact whale by a commercial whailing ship over 120 years ago and just never detonated. And because scientists knew the minimum age and size of whales targeted by whalers, they estimated this whale to be over 200 years old. This whale was born before the American Civil War. It was swimming in the Arctic Ocean while Abraham Lincoln was president. It survived the invention of the light bulb, two world wars, the moon landing, and the invention of the internet. All while casually swimming through freezing water with a harpoon lodged in its neck, confirming that this whale was over 200 years old immediately made the bowhead the longest living mammal on the entire planet. This isn't possible with blue whales. This isn't possible with sperm whales. In fact, no other whale on Earth comes even close to living half as long as this whale is, and especially not with a bomb tip in its neck. So, what is actually allowing this whale to not be able to die? To understand why a 200-year-old whale makes absolutely no sense, you have to look at how aging and disease actually work in living things. Every single time a cell in your body divides to create a new cell, it has to copy your DNA. And every single time it copies that DNA, there's a microscopic chance that it makes a mistake. Most of the time, these mistakes are harmless. But sometimes a cell mutates in a very specific way that causes it to start dividing out of control. That is cancer. [music] So logically, cancer is a numbers game. The more cells [music] you have, and the longer you live, the more times your cells have to divide, which means you have more chances to accidentally create a cancer cell. Humans have about 30 trillion cells. We get cancer pretty frequently. Now, look at the boowhead whale. These animals grow up to 60 ft long and can weigh over 100 tons. They have thousands of times more cells than a human being. If biology works the way it's supposed to, an animal with that many cells should be getting terminal cancer before it even grows up. Because they have so many cells dividing inside a 100 ton body, they essentially have billions of more chances to mutate every single day. We do have other animals on Earth that live for a very long time, like the Galapicus tortoise, which can easily clear 150 years, but tortoises are small. They don't have a massive amount of cells, and their bodies move incredibly slowly. The bow head is the size of a submarine. I mean, just look at this thing. It's massive. Realistically, a boowhead whale should be completely riddled with tumors by the time it turns 30. But they aren't. They're somehow completely avoiding the normal limits of aging and disease and living for over two centuries completely tumor free. So, how is this animal completely ignoring the rules of biology? Well, look at where they actually choose to live. And it's miserable. If you look at the migration patterns of almost every other large whale on Earth, they all do essentially the same thing. Humpback whales, grey whales, and blue whales will spend their summers feeding in cold water. But when winter hits, they completely abandon those feeding grounds. They swim thousands of miles south to places like Mexico, Hawaii, or the Caribbean to breed and raise their calves in warm, comfortable water. They're basically taking a giant biological vacation. The boowhead whale completely ignores this. They live in the Arctic Ocean and they never leave. They're the only baine whale on the planet that spends its entire life in the freezing waters of the Arctic. And this environment is genuinely miserable. Because salt water has a lower freezing point than fresh water, the water temperature in the Arctic actually drops below 32° F without turning to ice. The whales are swimming in liquid that's literally below the freezing point of normal water, which is not exactly ideal. During the winter, the sun doesn't rise for months. The entire ocean goes completely dark. The water is freezing and the surface is basically a death trap. But this miserable environment is actually the first step in how they live for 200 years. When you live in water this cold, your body is forced to adapt. The freezing temperatures mean the bohead's metabolism is incredibly slow. Their heart rate drops. Their physical movements are sluggish. Their body temperature is heavily regulated to conserve as much energy as physically possible. In biology, there's a general rule. To live a very long time, you have to live very slow. By staying in the freezing Arctic, the bowhead forces its entire biological system to run on a lower gear, which drastically reduces the amount of stress placed on their cells over time. But choosing to live in the freezing Arctic creates one massive issue because eventually you have to breathe. Whales are mammals. They don't have gills. No matter how deep they dive or how cold the water gets, they eventually have to come to the surface to breathe oxygen. And in the Arctic Ocean, the surface doesn't always exist. During the winter, millions of square miles of the ocean's surface freezes completely solid. The sea ice can easily reach over 2 ft thick. For any other whale, swimming under this ice means you're completely screwed. If you run out of breath and the surface above you is solid ice, you simply drown, which is a pretty massive design flaw for an animal that lives in the ocean. So, how does a bowhead whale breathe when the ocean has a roof on it? They smash through it. If you look at the skeleton of a boowhead whale, the proportions look almost comical. Their skull is absolutely massive. It makes up a full third of their entire body length. A 60 ft whale will have a 20ft long head. And this skull isn't just large. It's incredibly thick and shaped with a distant upward curve. They basically just have a solid rock as a head. Seriously, look at the skeleton. It genuinely just looks like a giant helmet. When a bowhead needs to breathe and the ocean is frozen over, they just find a spot where the ice is slightly thinner, angle their massive bodies upward, and accelerate towards the surface. They use the sheer momentum of their 100 ton body to slam the crown of their head directly into the bottom of the ice sheet. They can shatter through solid sea ice up to two feet thick just to take a breath. No other animal on Earth is capable of doing this. They'll literally head but a frozen ocean until it breaks. And because their blow holes are positioned at the very peak of this massive skull, they only need to crack a small hole in the ice to exhale, take a deep breath, and sink back down into the dark. But headbutting a frozen ocean only solves the breathing problem. It doesn't stop the fact that they're still swimming in literal ice water. Living your entire life in below freezing water means that your entire body heat is constantly being sucked away into the ocean. If a human falls in the Arctic Ocean, hypothermia sets in within minutes and you're dead shortly after or really if any normal mammal falls in. To survive this, the bowhead whale just grew a ridiculous amount of fat. All whales have blubber, which is a dense layer of fat that traps heat inside their bodies, but the bow head takes this to an entirely different extreme. The blubber can reach up to 2 ft thick. This is the thickest layer of fat on any animal on the planet. For comparison, a blue whale, which is significantly larger than a bowhead, only has blubber that's about a foot thick. The bowhead is walking around with double the insulation of the largest animal on Earth. This blubber is so dense and so thick that it completely isolates their internal organs from the freezing water outside. They can comfortably swim through sub-zero temperatures without their core body temperature dropping at all. But walking or I guess swimming around wrapped in 2 ft of solid fat actually provides an even crazier advantage that has nothing to do with the cold. It makes you practically impossible to eat. When you're a slowmoving 100 ton animal floating around in the ocean, you're eventually going to attract predators. And in the ocean, the only predator that actually poses a threat to large whales is the orca. Killer whales are pack hunters. They regularly hunt large whales by surrounding them and physically holding them underwater until they drown. But they just can't really do this to a boowhead. First of all, drowning a bowhead is incredibly difficult because their entire survival strategy is based on hiding under solid ice. When orcas attack, the bowhead will simply swim into dense pack ice where the orcas, who have smaller dorsal fins and no battering ram skulls, cannot follow without getting trapped themselves. But even if the orcas catch a bowhead in open water, they run into a huge physical problem. Orca's teeth are about 4 in long. Bowhead blubber is 24 in thick. So when an orca bites a boowhead whale, absolutely nothing happens. Their teeth aren't even long enough to reach the actual muscle or vital organs. They're just biting into a massive wall of fat. Now obviously orcas are smart. They know they can't easily kill a full-g grown adult. So they almost exclusively target calves or sick individuals. And even then, it's an exhausting fight that often ends with the bowhead simply swimming away into the ice. A fully grown boowhead is basically untouchable. They're too thick to be bitten, too strong to be drowned, and they hide in an environment that kills, well, literally everything else. You'd think that an animal this massive would need to hunt down huge schools of fish or large squid to survive. But chasing down fastmoving prey requires a ton of energy. And as we already established, the bowhead's entire strategy for living to 200 years old relies on conserving energy and moving slowly. So, the largest creature in the Arctic solves its food problem by eating the absolute smallest creatures in the ocean. Bowhead whales are filter feeders, kind of like blue whales. Instead of teeth, they have massive plates hanging down from the roofs of their mouths that look like this. This is called baine. And because the bow head has a skull that's 20t long, they also hold the record for the longest baine of any whale. Their baine plates can grow up to 13 ft long. When it's time to eat, the bowhead doesn't chase anything. They simply open their massive mouths and slowly swim forward. Water rushes in, passing through the baine plates, which act like a giant civ. The water filters out and millions of microscopic crustations called copapods get trapped in the bristles. The whale then uses its massive tongue to scrape the copapods off the baine and swallows them whole. They can eat up to two tons of these tiny creatures every single day, all without ever having to sprint, fight, or struggle for a meal. They just open their mouths and drift. It's the laziest yet most effective hunting strategy on Earth. All of this is impressive, but it's really just explaining the issues outside of their body. It still doesn't answer. How do these guys still not have thousands of tumors? A few years ago, scientists finally managed to sequence the entire genome of the boowhead whale. They wanted to know exactly what was happening inside their cells that allowed a 100 ton animal to avoid tumors for two centuries. And what they found was completely insane. It turns out boowhead whale cells are actively equipped with genetic tools that human beings simply don't have. Specifically, scientists found unique mutations in two major genes, the ERCC1 gene and the PCNA gene. In a human body, when a cell's DNA gets damaged, the body usually only has two options. It either forces the cells to self-destruct, or in bad cases, the cell ignores the damage, mutates, and eventually turns into cancer. Bowhead whale cells have a third option. They actually fix the damage. When their DNA gets damaged, these modified genes literally pause the cell division process. They stop the cell from multiplying, cut out the damaged section of the DNA code, and patch it with the correct sequence before allowing the cell to continue dividing. Their bodies are actively proofreading their own genetic code. If a cell starts to mutate towards cancer, the boowhead's immune system identifies the error and repairs the DNA before a tumor can even begin to form. Their massive size doesn't even matter because their cells are quite literally built to fix themselves. So, naturally, this brings up an incredibly obvious question. If we know exactly which genes allow the bowhead to repair its DNA and live for 200 years, why don't we just put these genes into humans? The idea of taking cancer resistant genes from a whale and applying them to human medicine sounds like the perfect solution. If we could repair our own DNA the way a bowhead does, we could theoretically cure cancer and extend the human lifespan well past 150 years. But realistically, doing this would come with some severe side effects. Because you can't just take one piece of a bowhead's biology without taking the rest of the package. The reason the bohead's DNA repair system works so well is because their cells divide incredibly slowly. These modified genes have plenty of time to find errors and fix them simply because the whale's body is running at a fraction of the speed of a human. If you put this system into a human, you'd have to drastically slow down our cell division, too. And cell division is what allows us to heal. If you've got a cut on your arm, it [music] might take months to heal. Broken bones would take years. And human children would take decades just to grow up. Furthermore, running a metabolism [music] that's slow means you'd constantly feel cold and exhausted. You wouldn't have the energy to run, jump, or live a normal human life. You might live to be 250 years old, [music] and you might never get cancer, but you'd spend those two centuries living like a rock, which [music] honestly doesn't sound like a great time. The entire lifespan is a massive trade-off. They get to live for 200 years, but they have to spend those 200 years moving slowly, living in freezing darkness, and conserving every ounce of energy they have. And even with all of those incredible adaptations, they're still not immortal. Something's out there still killing them. Despite all these crazy adaptations, bowhead whales do still die out in the wild. And ironically, the exact same thing that protects them from predators is usually what ends up killing them, the sea ice. The bowhead skull is incredibly powerful and as we discussed, they can easily smash through 2 feet of solid ice to get a breath of fresh air. But the Arctic Ocean is unpredictable. Weather patterns can shift rapidly and temperatures can plummet overnight. Sometimes the ice freezes much thicker than 2 ft. If a bowhead is swimming underneath a massive sheet of ice and they realize they're running out of air, they'll instinctively swim up and slam their head into the surface. But if their ice is 3 or 4 feet thick, the ice doesn't break. The whale is now trapped. They'll frantically search for a thinner spot or a natural crack in the ice. But if the frozen sheet stretches for miles, they physically cannot swim fast enough to find open water before their lungs give out. The exact same ice that keeps the orcas away ends up trapping them, and the whale simply drowns. This is the harsh reality of the Arctic. The environment is so extreme that even the animals perfectly adapted to it are constantly one mistake away from death. But for a long time, the ice wasn't actually their biggest threat. For millions of years, the boowhead whale survival plan worked perfectly. Be massive, have incredibly thick blubber, move slowly, and stay in the ice. But in the 1700s and 1800s, this exact set of evolutionary traits turned them into the most heavily targeted animal on the planet. When commercial whaling exploded as an industry, ships sailed all over the world hunting whales for their blubber, which was boiled down into oil to light the street lamps of Europe and America. And whalers quickly realized that the bowhead was the absolute perfect target. First, they were slow. A bowhead whale cruises at about 2 to 3 mph, making them incredibly easy for rowboats to chase down and harpoon. Second, they had the thickest blubber of any whale, meaning a single bowhead could yield an absurd amount of highquality oil. They also had the longest baine, which was highly valuable at the time for making corsets and umbrella ribs. But the biggest reason they were targeted came down to basic physics. When you kill a large whale with a harpoon, the body usually sinks. And if you're on a 19th century whailing ship, how are you supposed to haul a 100 ton sinking carcass from up from the bottom of the ocean using nothing but ropes and pulleys? But the bowhead had 2 ft of blubber. And blubber is less dense than water. When you kill a bowhead whale, it doesn't even sink. It floats perfectly on the surface, which makes them extremely convenient. Their thick armor, their slow speed, and their buoyancy, the exact traits that made them masters of the Arctic, made them completely defenseless against human ships. By the early 1900s, commercial whailing had absolutely decimated the bowhead population, pushing them to the absolute brink of extinction. They were built to survive orcas and ice, but not really harpoons. Eventually, the world moved on from whale oil. Petroleum was discovered, electricity became widespread, and commercial whailing of the boowhead was officially banned in the 20th century to prevent them from going completely extinct. And this is where their insane lifespan finally work to their advantage. Usually, when a species is pushed to the brink of extinction, it takes many, many generations for the population to recover. The few surviving animals have to breed, their children have to grow up and breed, and it takes centuries to rebuild the numbers. But the boowhead whale doesn't operate on a normal timeline. Because they lived for over 200 years, the whales didn't need to rely on dozens of new generations to rebuild their population. The exact same whales that survived the harpoons in the 1800s simply waited for the ships to leave and then went right back to reproducing. A female boowhead whale can continue having calves [music] well into her hundreds. Their population has bounced back incredibly well over the past century. And a huge part of that success is simply because the individuals were capable of outliving the era of human hunting. They basically just sat under the ice and went, "Yeah, let us know when they leave." And because of how long they live, the bowhead whale actually has a level of cultural complexity that makes them kind of weird. Bowhead whales are incredibly vocal. And I know other whales make loud sounds, too. But boowheads don't make simple clicks or calls like other whales. They're singing. And scientists who have recorded bowhead vocalizations have discovered that these songs are highly complex, featuring multiple different melodies, overlapping notes, and distant phrasing. It has been compared to hearing a jazz band improvising underwater. Just a 100 ton freezing cold jazz band. Today, the boowhead whale is facing a completely new threat, and it's one that their 200-year-old bodies aren't adapted to handle. The Arctic sea ice is melting. At first glance, you might think less ice would actually be a good thing. I mean, less ice means they don't have to smash their heads through a frozen surface just to breathe. But the ice is the only thing keeping them safe. As the ice coverage shrinks, the Arctic Ocean is opening up. And that means the orcas, who previously couldn't navigate the thick pack ice, are now able to travel much further north. The bowheads are losing their primary hiding spots, exposing their calves to significantly more predation from killer whales. Furthermore, the lack of ice means human ships are moving in. Commercial shipping lanes are now cutting directly through the Arctic, bringing massive cargo ships into waters that used to be completely silent. For an animal that relies on complex songs to communicate in the dock, the roar of massive ship propellers is completely blinding them. The environment they spent millions of years adapting to is changing, and you can't outlive a melting ocean. The bohead whale isn't anywhere near as famous as the blue whale, but it's arguably even more incredible. We're still learning things about them, and we don't actually know their true limits to age. Maybe it's possible that some live near 300 years instead, which would rival them with Greenland sharks. But in any case, these guys are probably one of the coolest whales, or even just animals on this planet. And hey, other whales are still cool, too, though.
fullTextVi: Năm 2007, một nhóm thợ săn Anupia ở phía bắc Alaska đã săn bắt cá đầu cung một cách hợp pháp cá voi ngoài khơi. Nhưng khi họ đang cắt sâu vào phần cổ của con cá voi, của họ dụng cụ va vào vật gì đó cứng. Họ đã va vào kim loại rắn. Nó hoàn toàn hợp nhất với mô xung quanh và rõ ràng là rất cũ. Họ gửi nó cho các nhà sử học để tìm hiểu chính xác nó là gì, và kết quả không có ý nghĩa gì. Vật thể này là một mũi tên lửa và nó được sản xuất ở New Bedford, Massachusetts vào năm 1880, điều đó có nghĩa là chiếc lao móc chính xác này đã được bắn vào chính xác con cá voi này một con tàu săn cá voi thương mại hơn 120 năm trước và chưa bao giờ phát nổ. Và bởi vì các nhà khoa học biết độ tuổi và kích thước tối thiểu của những con cá voi mà những người săn cá voi nhắm đến, họ ước tính con cá voi này đã hơn 200 tuổi. Con cá voi này được sinh ra trước Nội chiến Hoa Kỳ. Nó đang bơi ở Bắc Băng Dương khi Abraham Lincoln còn là tổng thống. Nó sống sót sau việc phát minh ra bóng đèn, hai cuộc chiến tranh thế giới, cuộc đổ bộ lên mặt trăng, và sự phát minh ra Internet. Trong khi thản nhiên bơi qua làn nước đóng băng với một chiếc lao móc ở cổ, xác nhận con cá voi này đã hơn 200 tuổi ngay lập tức khiến chú cá voi động vật có vú sống lâu nhất trên toàn hành tinh. Điều này là không thể với cá voi xanh. Điều này là không thể với cá nhà táng. Trên thực tế, không có con cá voi nào khác trên Trái đất có thể sống gần bằng một nửa miễn là con cá voi này và đặc biệt là không có đầu bom trong neck. Vậy điều gì thực sự đã khiến con cá voi này không thể chết? Để hiểu tại sao con cá voi 200 tuổi hoàn toàn vô nghĩa, bạn phải nhìn về cách lão hóa và bệnh tật thực sự diễn ra trong các sinh vật sống. Mỗi khi một tế bào trong cơ thể bạn phân chia để tạo ra một tế bào mới, nó phải sao chép DNA của bạn. Và mỗi lần nó sao chép DNA đó, sẽ có một cơ hội rất nhỏ phạm sai lầm. Hầu hết thời gian, những sai lầm này là vô hại. Nhưng đôi khi một tế bào đột biến theo một cách rất cụ thể khiến nó bắt đầu phân chia ngoài tầm kiểm soát. Đó là bệnh ung thư. [âm nhạc] Về mặt logic, ung thư là một trò chơi của những con số. Bạn càng có nhiều tế bào [âm nhạc] và bạn càng sống lâu thì càng có nhiều thời gian các tế bào của bạn phải phân chia, điều đó có nghĩa là bạn có nhiều cơ hội vô tình tạo ra một tế bào ung thư. Con người có khoảng 30 nghìn tỷ tế bào. Chúng ta bị ung thư khá thường xuyên. Bây giờ, hãy nhìn vào con cá voi đầu cong. Những con vật này dài tới 60 ft và có thể nặng hơn 100 tấn. Họ có số lượng tế bào gấp hàng nghìn lần so với con người. Nếu sinh học hoạt động theo đúng cách của nó thì một loài động vật có nhiều tế bào như vậy sẽ bị ung thư giai đoạn cuối trước khi nó lớn lên. Bởi vì chúng có rất nhiều tế bào phân chia bên trong cơ thể nặng 100 tấn nên về cơ bản chúng có thêm hàng tỷ cơ hội để đột biến mỗi ngày. Chúng ta có những loài động vật khác trên Trái đất sống rất lâu, giống như loài rùa Galapicus, có thể dễ dàng vượt qua 150 năm nhưng rùa rất nhỏ. Chúng không có số lượng lớn tế bào và cơ thể chúng di chuyển cực kỳ chậm. Đầu mũi tàu có kích thước bằng một chiếc tàu ngầm. Ý tôi là, hãy nhìn vào thứ này. Nó rất lớn. Trên thực tế, một con cá voi đầu cong phải có đầy đủ các khối u vào thời điểm nó bước sang tuổi 30. Nhưng họ không như vậy. Bằng cách nào đó, họ hoàn toàn tránh được những giới hạn thông thường của lão hóa và bệnh tật và sống vì hơn hai thế kỷ hoàn toàn không có khối u. Vậy làm thế nào loài vật này lại hoàn toàn phớt lờ các quy luật sinh học? Chà, hãy nhìn vào nơi họ thực sự chọn để sống. Và thật khốn khổ. Nếu bạn nhìn vào mô hình di cư của hầu hết các loài cá voi lớn khác trên Trái đất, về cơ bản tất cả đều làm điều tương tự. Cá voi lưng gù, cá voi xám và cá voi xanh sẽ trải qua mùa hè kiếm ăn trong giá lạnh Nước. Nhưng khi mùa đông đến, chúng hoàn toàn bỏ rơi những bãi kiếm ăn đó. Chúng bơi hàng ngàn dặm về phía nam tới những nơi như Mexico, Hawaii hay vùng Caribe để sinh sản và nuôi dưỡng bê con trong nước ấm và thoải mái. Về cơ bản họ đang có một kỳ nghỉ sinh học khổng lồ. Cá voi đầu cong hoàn toàn phớt lờ điều này. Họ sống ở Bắc Băng Dương và không bao giờ rời đi. Chúng là loài cá voi baine duy nhất trên hành tinh dành toàn bộ cuộc đời của mình trong vùng nước đóng băng của Bắc Cực. Và môi trường này thực sự khốn khổ. Vì nước mặn có nhiệt độ đóng băng thấp hơn nước ngọt nên nhiệt độ của nước ở Bắc Cực thực sự giảm xuống dưới 32°F mà không chuyển thành băng. Những con cá voi đang bơi trong chất lỏng có nhiệt độ thấp hơn điểm đóng băng bình thường theo đúng nghĩa đen nước, điều này không thực sự lý tưởng. Vào mùa đông, mặt trời không mọc trong nhiều tháng. Toàn bộ đại dương chìm trong bóng tối hoàn toàn. Nước đang đóng băng và bề mặt về cơ bản là một cái bẫy chết người.
